overview: Ngarrindjeri communities connect the lower Murray, lakes, Coorong and Sea Country through law, kinship, food and cultural responsibility. Fishing technology, feather flowers and David Unaipon's papers reveal skill and invention in different settings. Their history continues through dispossession, environmental disruption, community teaching and public advocacy.

periods.title: Raukkan, adaptation and continuing cultural life
periods.summary: The mission established at Point McLeay in 1859 became part of a continuing community history at Raukkan. Families developed enterprises and artistic work under colonial constraints; later teaching and advocacy carried knowledge into new institutions.

items.text: The community's Sea Country Plan describes Tendi as a council that makes and interprets Ngarrindjeri law. Ngartji relationships with particular animals and plants bring obligations to care for them and their habitats.

Fish, shellfish, waterbirds and plants supported settled life and gatherings. Nets made from bulrush fibers, bone or shell hooks, stone traps and woven weirs show different ways of working with water and animal behavior.

Bark canoes, reed rafts and floating platforms supported work on the water. Food storage and smoke-drying fish helped supply gatherings and exchange with neighboring communities. These practices joined making, preservation and social relationships.

sections.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge

items.text: A bouquet made at Point McLeay in the 1920s, now in the National Museum of Australia, uses feathers from pelicans and other Coorong birds. Makers drew dye from crepe paper soaked in water, then colored the feathers. The object records skilled adaptation of available materials.

The Point McLeay mission began in 1859 on land too small for the families moved there. Ngarrindjeri people developed fishing, boat making, wool washing, weaving and other enterprises. Feather flowers provided income while also carrying ecological and artistic knowledge.

Changes to river flows and wetlands affect materials as well as food. The museum account describes freshwater sedges used in weaving becoming scarcer. Maintaining a craft therefore also depends on the health and accessibility of the places that supply it.

sections.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers

items.text: Patent 15624, dated 3 September 1909, records David Unaipon's improved mechanical motion device. Applied to sheep shearing, it converted rotary movement into straight-line motion. The patent and accompanying diagrams provide a specific record of an inventor working on an industrial problem.

In an April 1914 letter to Herbert Basedow, Unaipon asked for financial help to develop his machine. A following memorandum offered conditional government assistance. These papers reveal the difficulty of obtaining support; a patent alone does not demonstrate profitable manufacture.

Unaipon also collected and wrote stories. Material from his manuscript appeared under William Ramsay Smith's name in 1930. Work with Unaipon's descendants later restored his authorship in the 2001 publication of Legendary Tales of the Australian Aborigines.

Elder Ellen Trevorrow teaches weaving and cultural storytelling at Camp Coorong. Her work connects the making of baskets and sculpture with learning across generations. Participants learn through shared activity and conversation as well as looking at finished objects.

Camp Coorong activities also include walks with Elders to learn about animals, food plants and Country. Such teaching connects practical knowledge with the responsibility to understand and care for the places where it is used.

The Sea Country Plan describes colonial land loss and mission pressure on language and belief. Its response is continuing Ngarrindjeri participation in decisions about land and waters, with cultural responsibilities informing future management.

ending.text: Ngarrindjeri people and cultural life continue. Dispossession and changes to rivers and wetlands damaged livelihoods and access to Country, but Raukkan, Camp Coorong and living artistic practices show continuing community history. There is no single fall year or successor state that describes that experience.
